problem_statement: The paper frames portfolio optimization as choosing an allocation of assets that satisfies desired return and risk conditions, and in this work it focuses specifically on maximizing the Sharpe ratio. It treats the portfolio weights as the decision variables for the allocation problem.
problem_statement_quotes:
The Portfolio Optimization task has long been studied in the Finan-
cial Services literature as a procedure to identify the basket of assets
that satisfy desired conditions on the expected return and the associated
risk.

In this work we focus on maximizing a speciﬁc objective function - the Sharpe ratio, deﬁned
as ratio between the expected return of a portfolio µ and the square root of
its variance σ2.

The aim of Portfolio Optimization is to determine an assets allocation (portfo-
lio) able to maximize or minimize a desired objective function.
classical_baseline: The paper compares its QUBO approach against the classical quadratic formulation of the Max-Sharpe problem, and also against the classical strategy implemented in PyPortfolioOpt that solves the formulation from Cornuejols and Tütüncü. It also contrasts its new formulation with the proxy approach from Venturelli and Kondratyev.
classical_baseline_quotes:
In this work, we take the classical quadratic formulation that can be
employed to solve the maximization of the Sharpe Ratio, hereafter called Max
Sharpe, and build the corresponding QUBO formulation.

In Figure 2 we compare the results with the solution found by the classical strategy
implemented in the PyPortfolioOpt library [21], which solves the problem as
formulated in [20].

The approach proposed in [19] to tackle the Max-Sharpe problem focuses
on ﬁnding suitable coeﬃcients for the QUBO formulation (5) that reﬂect
the Sharpe Ratio maximization.
classical_difficulty: The paper says the Sharpe-ratio objective is nonlinear, and that the proxy QUBO does not exactly equal the true Sharpe-ratio maximization. It also notes that discretization trades off fidelity against a larger number of variables, which can make solvers perform worse.
classical_difficulty_quotes:
On the other hand, it must be noted that such a formulation is used as
a proxy for the Sharpe Ratio, as its optimization does not mathematically
equate to the maximization of the Sharpe Ratio as it is deﬁned (ref. 1).

Building on this consideration, we take the quadratic model for the Max-
Sharpe problem as introduced in [20] and propose a new formulation by
implementing it as a QUBO model.
extraction_notes: Motivation is explicit in abstract and introduction; paper is mainly algorithmic but does state the finance problem clearly.
